title: Kristopher Boulton on Theory of Instruction
author: Zach Groshell
summary: In this Direct Instruction Podcast interview, recorded at the National DI Conference in Eugene, Zach Groshell talks with maths educator Kristopher Boulton about Engelmann and Carnine's Theory of Instruction. Boulton distinguishes a theory of learning from a theory of instruction: the first can be rigorous and still say nothing about how to sequence teaching on a Monday, so the two must be complementary but distinct. He explains why the book is so hard to read, citing Rob Dixon's point that its authors were founding a new discipline and had to invent its language, while drawing examples from reading, maths and classification. Because subjects differ in their mix of facts, routines and concepts, his team now works only on mathematics to make the abstract ideas concrete. He and his wife Naveen came to DI by different routes: she saw a program's design emerge across lessons 30, 40 and 50, while he came through the theory and built his own sequences for content with no existing DI program. The post is a transcript of a podcast episode, archived because the complete transcript is supplied.
points: A theory of learning explains how people learn but does not tell a teacher how to sequence examples, which is the job of a theory of instruction.

Theory of Instruction is hard to read because it invented its own vocabulary and mixes examples from reading, maths and concept classification, so subject-specific application is the practical route in.
Subjects have different epistemologies, with maths routine-heavy and history fact-heavy, so how the theory is applied changes by subject.
A DI program's design is only visible across many lessons, as Naveen discovered at lessons 30, 40 and 50, which argues for judging programs over weeks, not single lessons.
Boulton designs his own maths sequences for upper-level topics that no DI program covers, built from the theory plus cognitive science and variation theory.
quotes: But you can have a robust and rigorous science or theory of learning, and still it won't tell you anything about how to teach. It doesn't tell you how to teach sequences on Monday, if that's what I'm going to teach my kids, for example.
That's where you need a science or theory of instruction. And whatever that is, it needs to marry up with your theory of learning. Those two things need to be complementary, but they are distinct.

He says what Doug Carnine and Zig Engelmann were trying to do was make sense of everything that was in their own heads — that they'd developed over the previous 20 years or more — and in so doing, they were giving birth to a brand-new discipline and a new field of inquiry. And because of that, they essentially had to invent language.
Mathematics is very, very routine-heavy; biology and, say, history are very, very fact-heavy. And so how you apply it in aggregate changes quite a lot.

It doesn't happen immediately, because you can't see it in one lesson, but as she was teaching it over weeks and months, she started to see how things in lessons 30, 40, 50 were all linking together with the previous lessons that had come through.
Nobody cares. They sort of care, but they don't care institutionally, because those kids are never going to sit the exam; they're never going to show up in any of the performance metrics.

But they clicked into place in a way where I devised and created it myself, based on everything I'd read, as opposed to delivering a pre-existing DI program. That's really helpful, because there are no pre-existing DI programs for most of higher-level mathematics.
